title: Drift in small and large populations

stimulus.title: Two wildflower populations
stimulus.html: A wildflower has purple or white flowers, controlled by one gene; the allele for white flowers is recessive. Flower color makes no difference to which plants are visited by pollinators, survive or set seed. Population 1 has about 5,000 flowering plants in a large meadow. Population 2 has about 25 flowering plants on a rocky hilltop 30 km away, and no pollen or seeds pass between the two. In 1990 the frequency of the white allele was 0.30 in both populations.

parts.label: a

rubric.point: Describes genetic drift as a random (chance) change in allele frequencies from one generation to the next, not caused by differences in fitness.
accept: random change in allele frequencies over generations
changes in allele frequency due to chance in which individuals reproduce and which alleles they pass on
evolution by chance rather than by selection

parts.sample: Genetic drift is a random change in a population's allele frequencies from one generation to the next. It happens because which individuals reproduce, and which of their alleles end up in their offspring, is partly a matter of chance, not because one allele raises fitness.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the frequency of the white allele is expected to change more in population 2 than in population 1 over the next 20 generations.

rubric.point: Explains that the alleles passed to each generation are a sample of the parents' alleles, and a small sample (25 plants, 50 copies) is more likely to differ from the parents' frequencies by chance than a large one (5,000 plants), so drift is stronger in the small population.
accept: chance events have a bigger effect when few individuals reproduce
in a small population, a few plants failing to reproduce changes the allele frequency a lot
sampling error is larger in small samples

parts.sample: Each generation's alleles are a random sample of the alleles of the plants that reproduce. Population 2 has only about 50 copies of the gene, so by chance its sample can easily contain many more or many fewer white alleles than before; if a few plants with white alleles happen to set no seed, the frequency shifts a lot. In population 1, with about 10,000 copies, chance gains and losses mostly cancel out, so the frequency stays close to 0.30.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict how the genetic variation for flower color in population 2 will change over many generations if the population stays small and isolated. Justify your prediction.

rubric.point: Predicts that genetic variation will decrease, justified by drift eventually fixing or losing an allele (frequency reaching 1 or 0), after which only one allele, and one flower color, remains (fewer heterozygotes).
accept: variation decreases because drift will eventually lose the white or the purple allele
one allele will become fixed, so all plants will have the same genotype

parts.sample: Genetic variation will decrease. In a small population drift keeps moving the allele frequency at random, and once it reaches 0 or 1, the lost allele cannot come back without new mutation or gene flow. Over many generations one allele is likely to be lost, leaving every plant with the same flower-color genotype.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Bees begin to carry pollen between the two populations every year. Predict the effect on the difference between the white-allele frequencies of the two populations, and justify your prediction.

rubric.point: Predicts that the difference will decrease (the frequencies become more similar), because gene flow moves alleles between the populations, mixing their gene pools; it would also bring back an allele that population 2 had lost.
accept: the frequencies will become more alike because of gene flow
pollen movement brings population 1's alleles into population 2, pulling its frequency toward 0.30
gene flow counteracts drift in the small population

parts.sample: The difference will shrink. Pollen carried by bees is gene flow: it moves alleles between the populations, so the two gene pools mix. Because population 1 is so much larger, the small population's allele frequency will be pulled toward the large population's, and any allele population 2 had lost by drift can be brought back.
